title: DNAME Redirection in the DNS
summary: The DNAME record redirects a whole subtree of the DNS: every name ending in a given suffix is mapped to the same part of another tree. It obsoletes RFC 2672 and updates RFC 3363.

plainLanguage.summary: A DNAME record points a whole branch of DNS names at another branch. When a lookup finds one, the part of the name below the record is swapped for the target name and the search carries on there. One record can therefore redirect thousands of names at once, which is what makes it useful for renaming an organization or renumbering a network.

questions: what is a dns dname record
why are wildcard dname records discouraged
subtitle: A DNS record that redirects a whole subtree of names to another part of the name tree.

tldr.problem: A CNAME redirects one name, so moving a branch of the DNS tree or renumbering a network needs a CNAME at every name, and the names below the CNAME owner cannot hold records of their own.
tldr.mechanism: A DNAME record names a suffix and a target. When a lookup reaches a name below the owner, the matching labels are replaced with the target's labels and the search continues in the new part of the tree.
tldr.outcome: One record redirects an entire subtree, which makes organizational renaming, classless reverse delegation and network renumbering possible without touching the data in the target zone, and the record is now standardised by RFC 6672 in place of RFC 2672.

today:
RFC 6672 is a Proposed Standard and obsoletes RFC 2672, the original DNAME specification. It also updates RFC 3363, which had deprecated the use of DNAME records in the IPv6 reverse tree; that deprecation is dropped.

The revision did not change the wire format or the handling of DNAME records. It clarified the substitution rules, confirmed that there is no EDNS signalling for DNAME compression, changed the TTL of a synthesized CNAME from zero to the TTL of the DNAME, made CNAME synthesis on behalf of clients a requirement for recursive caching servers, and added rules for dynamic updates that add a DNAME or a CNAME where the other already exists.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
DNAME is a DNS resource record type originally defined in RFC 2672. It provides redirection from a part of the DNS name tree to another part of the DNS name tree.

The DNAME record and the CNAME record both cause a lookup to return data for a domain name different from the one queried. The difference is that a CNAME directs the lookup of data at its owner to another single name, whereas a DNAME directs lookups for data at descendants of its owner's name to corresponding names under a different, single, node of the tree. If a zone contains a DNAME at example.com indicating that all queries under example.com are directed to example.net, a lookup for foo.example.com returns to the top of the lookup process with the new query name foo.example.net, and a lookup for www.foo.example.com becomes www.foo.example.net.

DNAME was conceived to help with the problem of maintaining address-to-name mappings in a context of network renumbering. With a careful setup, a renumbering event causes no change to the authoritative server that holds the address-to-name mappings; classless reverse address space delegations are an example in practice. Another use is aliasing name spaces, so that subtrees of the DNS can contain the same information, for instance punycode alternates for domain spaces.

This revision does not change the wire format or the handling of DNAME records. It adds discussion of problems that may be encountered when using DNAME.
sections.plainLanguage: A CNAME sends one name to one other name. A DNAME sends a whole branch of names to another branch, by swapping the part of the name that sits below the record. The point is that one record can then move thousands of names at once, and the zone that used to hold the names does not have to change.

sections.title: The DNAME Resource Record
sections.content:
The DNAME RR has the mnemonic DNAME and type code 39 in decimal. It is CLASS-insensitive. Its RDATA is made up of a single field, <target>, which contains a fully qualified domain name that must be sent in uncompressed form. The target field must be present, and its presentation format is that of a domain name. The presentation format of the record is <owner> <ttl> <class> DNAME <target>.

The effect of the DNAME record is the substitution of the record's target for its owner name, as a suffix of a domain name. The substitution is applied to all names below the owner name of the DNAME, and it has to be applied for every DNAME record found in the resolution process, which allows fairly lengthy valid chains of DNAME records.
sections.plainLanguage: The record is very small. It holds one field, the target name, and the rest is the usual owner name, time to live and class that every DNS record has. The target must be written out in full rather than abbreviated, and the owner name may be abbreviated as usual.

sections.title: The DNAME Substitution
sections.content:
The substitution happens when the server, matching down label by label inside a zone, finds a node that owns a DNAME resource record. The name being sought may be the original query name, or a name reached by following a CNAME, or a name reached by an earlier DNAME. As with a CNAME or an NS record set, the DNAME is processed before the desired domain name is found.

The substitution replaces the suffix labels of the name being sought that match the owner name of the DNAME with the string of labels in the RDATA field. The matching labels end with the root label in all cases, and only whole labels are replaced, so a query for ab.example.com against a DNAME owned by b.example.com does not match at all.

DNAMEs can form loops, just as CNAMEs can, and DNAMEs and CNAMEs can chain together to form a loop. A single corner case DNAME can also form a loop. Resolvers and servers should be cautious about the resources they devote to a query, but they should also know that fairly long chains of DNAMEs may be valid.

The domain name can get too long during substitution. If the target name of the DNAME is 250 octets in length and an incoming query has a first label over 5 octets in length, the result would be a name over 255 octets. In that case the server returns an RCODE of YXDOMAIN, and the DNAME record and its signature, if the zone is signed, are included in the answer as proof.
sections.plainLanguage: When the lookup reaches the record, the resolver takes the part of the name that matched the record and replaces it with the target. The swap is done on whole labels only, so a name that merely looks similar is left alone. The new name is then looked up in the normal way.

sections.title: Names Next to and Below a DNAME Record
sections.content:
Unlike a CNAME, a DNAME redirects names subordinate to its owner name; the owner name of a DNAME is not redirected itself. The domain name that owns a DNAME may have other resource record types, except DNAMEs, CNAMEs, or other types that carry restrictions on what they can coexist with. When the QTYPE matches a type also owned by the owner name, the response is sourced from the owner name, so a QTYPE of ANY returns the available types at the owner name and not at the target name.

A DNAME must not appear at the same owner name as an NS record unless that owner name is the zone apex. If it is not the apex, the NS record signifies a delegation point, and the DNAME must in that case appear below the zone cut, at the zone apex of the child zone. If a DNAME is present at the zone apex, the customary SOA and NS records are still needed there as well, and such a DNAME cannot be used to mirror a zone completely, because it does not mirror the zone apex.

Resource records must not exist at any subdomain of the owner of a DNAME. To get the contents for names subordinate to that owner name, the DNAME redirection has to be invoked and the resulting target queried. A server may refuse to load a zone that has data at such a subdomain; if it does load the zone, those names are occluded in the sense of RFC 2136. DNAME is a singleton type, so only one DNAME is allowed per name and no CNAMEs can exist at that name, which means there is never any doubt about which redirection to follow.

These rules also allow DNAME records to be queried through caches that are RFC 1034 compliant and DNAME unaware.
sections.plainLanguage: The name that holds the DNAME is not itself redirected, so it can still carry other records such as mail exchanger entries. Nothing may be stored below it, because everything there is reached through the redirect instead. And there can be only one DNAME at a name, with no CNAME beside it, so a lookup never has a choice of which redirect to take.

sections.title: Wildcards and Dynamic Update
sections.content:
The use of DNAME together with wildcards is discouraged, so records of the form *.example.com DNAME example.net should not be used. The interaction between the expansion of the wildcard and the redirection of the DNAME is non-deterministic. Because the processing is non-deterministic, DNSSEC validating resolvers may not be able to validate a wildcarded DNAME. A server may give a warning that the behaviour is unspecified if such a record is loaded, and may refuse it, refuse to load the zone, or refuse dynamic updates.

DNAME records can be added, changed and removed in a zone with dynamic update transactions. Adding a DNAME to a zone occludes any domain names that may exist under it. If a dynamic update message tries to add a DNAME with a given owner name and a CNAME is associated with that name, the server must ignore the DNAME. If a DNAME is already associated with that name, it is replaced with the new one. If a CNAME is added where a DNAME is associated with the name, the CNAME must be ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: A wildcard DNAME behaves unpredictably, because the wildcard and the redirect can both match the same name and the order in which they are applied is not fixed. The document advises against them. Adding a DNAME to a zone by dynamic update also hides any names that were below it.

sections.title: CNAME Synthesis
sections.content:
A server performing a DNAME substitution includes the relevant DNAME record in the answer section in all cases: when the DNAME is being employed as a substitution instruction, and when the DNAME itself matches the QTYPE and its owner name matches the QNAME. When the owner name matches the QNAME and the QTYPE matches another type owned there, the DNAME is not included.

A CNAME record with a Time to Live equal to the corresponding DNAME record is synthesized and included in the answer section when the DNAME is employed as a substitution instruction, and the owner name of that CNAME is the QNAME of the query. The DNSSEC specification says the synthesized CNAME does not have to be signed. The signed DNAME has an RRSIG, and a validating resolver can check the CNAME against the DNAME record and validate the signature over the DNAME record.

Servers must be able to answer a query for a synthesized CNAME. Like other query types, this invokes the DNAME, and then the server synthesizes the CNAME and places it in the answer section. If the server is a cache, the synthesized CNAME's TTL should be equal to the decremented TTL of the cached DNAME.

Resolvers must be able to handle a synthesized CNAME with a TTL of zero, or with a value equal to the TTL of the corresponding DNAME record, because some older authoritative server implementations set the TTL of synthesized CNAMEs to zero. A TTL of zero means the CNAME can be discarded immediately after processing the answer.
sections.plainLanguage: Most resolvers only understand CNAME, so a server that applies a DNAME also makes up a CNAME pointing at the substituted name and puts it in the answer. The made-up CNAME is not signed, because the server does not sign online; the DNAME record that comes with it is signed, and that is what a validating resolver checks.

sections.title: DNSSEC and DNAME
sections.content:
In any response, a signed DNAME record indicates a non-terminal redirection of the query. There might or might not be a server-synthesized CNAME in the answer section, and if there is, the CNAME will never be signed. For a DNSSEC validator, verification of the DNAME record and then confirmation that the CNAME was properly synthesized is sufficient proof.

In any negative response, the NSEC or NSEC3 record type bitmap should be checked to see that there was no DNAME that could have been applied. If the DNAME bit in the type bitmap is set and the query name is a subdomain of the closest encloser that is asserted, then DNAME substitution should have been done but was not, which is what a forged reply assembled from existing records looks like. The document gives two worked examples: a reply whose NSEC record shows that the queried name needed to be redirected, which a validator can only see as bogus if it understands the DNAME bit, and the same NSEC record with a query name that is not redirected, which validates correctly.

A response can contain a chain of DNAME and CNAME redirections, and only if every step in the chain is secure can the Authentic Data bit be set for the response. If one step is bogus, the result is bogus.

DNAME redirects queries elsewhere, which may affect security based on policy and on the security status of the zone holding the DNAME and of the redirection zone. For validating resolvers, the lowest security status of the links in the chain of CNAME and DNAME redirections is applied to the result. A validating resolver that accepts wildcarded DNAMEs creates security issues, because the processing is non-deterministic and the substituted CNAME has no signature, so the resolver may choose a different result from the one the server meant and end up at the wrong destination. A validating resolver must understand DNAME.
sections.plainLanguage: DNSSEC signs the DNAME record but not the CNAME the server makes up from it, so a validator checks the signed record and works out the substitution for itself. It also has to look at the denial-of-existence records, because those show whether a name should have been redirected, which is how a forged reply gets caught.

sections.title: Examples of DNAME Use in a Zone
sections.content:
Section 6 gives three examples of DNAME use in a zone. The first is an organizational renaming. If an organization with the domain name FROBOZZ.EXAMPLE.NET became part of an organization with the domain name ACME.EXAMPLE.COM, the old zone can hold a DNAME pointing at frobozz-division.acme.example.com. A recursive query for www.frobozz.example.net then returns the DNAME record and the relevant records for www.frobozz-division.acme.example.com. The MX record at the zone apex is not redirected and has to be repeated in the target zone, and the services at the target have to recognise and handle the aliases.

The second is classless delegation of shorter prefixes. The scheme for in-addr.arpa delegation can be extended to prefixes shorter than 24 bits by using DNAME records, so the prefix 192.0.8.0/22 is delegated with an NS record for 8/22 and DNAME records at 8, 9, 10 and 11 pointing at 8.8/22, 9.8/22, 10.8/22 and 11.8/22. The advisory remarks in RFC 2317 about the choice of the slash character apply here as well.

The third is network renumbering support. If IPv4 network renumbering were common, DNAME records could be used instead of NS records to delegate, so that the address space 190.189.0.0/16 assigned to an ISP could be changed without altering the zone data describing how the ISP and its customers use that space. The document notes that renumbering IPv4 networks is currently so arduous a task that updating the DNS is only a small part of the labour, so this scheme may have low value, but it is hoped that renumbering will be quite different in IPv6 and that the DNAME mechanism may play a useful part.
sections.plainLanguage: The document shows DNAME doing three jobs: moving an organization to a new domain name, delegating a reverse zone for a network larger than a class C, and keeping the DNS steady while an ISP renumbers its address space. In each case the zone that describes the old names stays where it is and the redirect does the work.
